caseno: Appeal from Appellate decree No. 620 of 1962.
lawyer:
N.B. Chowdhury, Advocate-------For appellants. 
Abdus Salam, Advocate-------For Respondent No. 1.
parties:
Mahendra Kumar Roy and others -------- Appellants.
Vs.
Akbar Molla and others---------- Respondents.
full_judgment: 10. Mr. Chowdhury, has next argued that there was no evidence that the property in Matangini's hands was not sufficient to meet her needs. The short answer to this argument would be that had it been so, Matangini would not have landed in the Government Langarkhana due to successive failure of crops. Nor, does it appear that the plaintiffs who are now claiming the property as reversionary heirs, came forward to help at the time of her distress, in which case she would not have to seek shelter in the Langarkhana. Mr. Chowdhury has also argued that there is no evidence to prove her legal necessity. It appears that the courts below have found that there was famine in 1350 and there were successive crop failures in 1348 and 1349 and she had to transfer the suit lands to her father. These facts have also been admitted by the plaintiff's witnesses and are, in my opinion, direct evidence of the state of things then prevailing and of her actual financial position which compelled her to part with the suit land for her own maintenance and living. Mr. Chowdhury has also argued that the courts below have arrived at findings on circumstances and surmises which were no substitute for legal evidence. It is true that circumstances themselves are not sufficient to prove or disprove a case. But in the facts and circumstances of the instant case, If feel, circumstances do have more importance than can ordinarily be presumed. The Courts in their efforts to do justice can certainly take into consideration the attending circumstances and draw reasonable inferences from them, if the ends of justice required their consideration and those were not incompatible with the pleadings. In the instant case Matangini was dead, her father Tenu Mondal was not coming forward despite due summons. In such circumstances I, feel that the courts below were perfectly justified in taking into consideration the attending circumstances and draw reasonable inferences from them. It is true that legal necessity has to be proved and mere recital in the deed of alienation is not sufficient proof. If however owing to lapse of time direct evidence of the facts and circumstances recited has disappeared) the recitals acquire importance. The lapse of time will save the alienee from an adverse inference arising from the sketchy nature of evidence adduced by him and will allow presumptions to fill in details in the evidence which had been obliterated by the passage of time. This view of mine finds support from the Full Bench decision in the case of Marla Sub. rahmannam Vs. Chilikani China Soomrayya, reported in AIR 1950 Madras 514 (FB). In reply, Mr. Salam has cited the case of Baraju Bala Ghose and others Vs. Lal Behari Mitra, reported in 6 DLR 225., wherein it was held that if the transactions are impeached the burden lies on the transferees to prove either that there was legal necessity in fact or that proper and bonafide enquiries were made by the transferees as to the existence of necessity and they did all that was reasonable to satisfy themselves as to the existence of necessity. The transferees have either of the two alternatives to establish. In this case the evidence on record clearly show that the defendants made proper and bonafide enquiries as to the existence of necessity and that they did all that was reasonable to satisfy themselves as to the existence of the legal necessity. Mr. Salam, has next cited the case of Ramappa Gudadapa Gudadannavar Vs. Chandanagouds Neelangouda, reported in AIR 1960, Mysore page 260-where-in it was held, that the question of legal necessity is one of fact and the High Court will not interfere with the findings in Second Appeal. In the case of Jamuna Chowdhury and seats Vs. Ramanup Singh and others, reported in AIR 1960 Patna at page 182, it was held that where there was no necessity in fact but it was proved that there was in fact representation of necessity and the alliance after making proper and bonafide enquiries satisfied himself as best as he could that such necessity existed, then the actual existence of a legal necessity would not be a condition precedent to the validity of the sale. Mr. Salam has also cited the case of Madan Gopal & others Vs. Maran Bepari and ors reported in 21 DLR (SC) 448 where it has been held that the Supreme Court would not interfere on the question of fact which is based on findings of fact by the courts below.
